video_metadata.working_title: CALIFORNIA 1985 Cold Case Solved After 25 Years — Justice for the Lost Women of South LA
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: How ten murders of Black women and girls in South Los Angeles (1985–2007) and the survival of Enietra Washington were finally tied to one man through California's familial DNA program and a pizza crust collected by an undercover officer, and why the community says police took far too long.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into quiet outrage at a system that did not warn the women at risk, then bittersweet justice

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Lonnie David Franklin Jr. (convicted; died on death row 2020)
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: Born 1952 (background; consistent with reported ages 57 at arrest in 2010, 63 at conviction in 2016, 67 at death in 2020) [NBC News 2010; AP 2016; CDCR 2020]
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Former City of Los Angeles sanitation worker (garbage collector) and onetime garage attendant for the Los Angeles Police Department; neighbors knew him as a mechanic who worked on cars in his driveway [AP via Inquirer.net 2016; NBC News 2010]
protagonist.location: A house on 81st Street in South Los Angeles [NBC News 2010]
protagonist.physical_description: Not used in script beyond public mugshots; Enietra Washington's 1988 description was challenged by the defense on height and pock-marks [ABC7 2016]
protagonist.background_brief: Served in the U.S. Army in Germany; in 1974 near Stuttgart he and two other soldiers attacked a 17-year-old girl, and a German court convicted all three men (penalty-phase testimony, 2016) [ABC7 2016; AP 2016]. General discharge 1975 (single-sourced, fan wiki; not used).
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not speculated. Prosecutor Beth Silverman told jurors the murders 'followed a pattern' and that he targeted women made vulnerable by the crack-cocaine epidemic [AP via Inquirer.net 2016].
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: To neighbors he was a friendly mechanic who often stopped to chat as he tinkered with cars in the driveway of his mint-green house on 81st Street [NBC News 2010].
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: 'Grim Sleeper', coined by LA Weekly reporter Christine Pelisek in 2008 because of the apparent 13-to-14-year gap between 1988 and 2002 [KQED; Pelisek; Wikipedia]

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Black women and girls of South Los Angeles, many affected by poverty and the crack epidemic; plus women whose photos were found in his home and uncharged deaths presented at the penalty phase
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: 10 murders + 1 attempted murder convicted; 3 more deaths (Georgia Mae Thomas 43, Sharon Dismuke 21, Inez Warren 28) presented at penalty phase without charges; 2 missing women (Ayellah Marshall 18, Rolenia Morris 29) whose ID cards were found in his garage; about 180 photos of about 160 women released in Dec 2010
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Murder, survival with lifelong trauma, families waiting up to 31 years

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Det. Dennis Kilcoyne
characters.role_in_story: LAPD detective who led the 2007 task force
characters.key_actions_they_took: Ran the investigation from 2007; publicly described the failed 2008 familial search and the 2010 hit; said several serial killers operated in the same area in the 1980s
characters.notable_quotes: 'learned of a man that as we know now turned out to be a direct relative of our suspect' (Stanford Law blog, 2010)

characters.name: Christine Pelisek
characters.key_actions_they_took: Revealed the secret task force in August 2008, coined 'Grim Sleeper', reported that families had not been told

characters.name: Margaret Prescod
characters.role_in_story: Founder of the Black Coalition Fighting Back Serial Murders (1986)
characters.key_actions_they_took: Weekly protests at LAPD headquarters; pushed reward increase; decades of criticism
characters.notable_quotes: 'We are saddened that Lonnie Franklin died without providing information on the scores of women he killed.' (KPFK, 2020)

characters.name: Jerry Brown
characters.key_actions_they_took: Adopted the first state familial DNA search policy (2008)
characters.notable_quotes: 'In the face of a multitude of objections, we've crafted a balanced policy to respect the rights of citizens and at the same time deploy the most powerful DNA search technology available' (CA OAG, 2010)

characters.name: Beth Silverman
characters.key_actions_they_took: Tried the case 2016; chose not to add uncharged killings to avoid more delay

characters.name: Seymour Amster
characters.key_actions_they_took: Challenged DNA and ballistics, suggested other attackers, sought a new trial

characters.name: Judge Kathleen Kennedy
characters.key_actions_they_took: Denied new trial; imposed death sentence Aug 10, 2016
characters.notable_quotes: 'This is not a sentence of vengeance.' (AP, 2016)

characters.name: Porter Alexander Jr. and Mary Alexander
characters.notable_quotes: 'He took my baby' (CSM); 'We got what we came to get, a just verdict' / 'I'm glad I lived to see it. It's a long time coming.' (AP); Mary: 'It didn't come when I wanted but it came right on time' (AP)

characters.name: Christopher Franklin
characters.key_actions_they_took: Convicted on a felony weapons charge in 2009; his DNA in the state database produced the familial lead. He was not involved in the murders.

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.what_is_happening: Enietra Washington, about 30, walking to a friend's house, accepts a ride from a man in an orange Ford Pinto
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: She is shot in the chest, assaulted, photographed and pushed out of the car, and survives
the_moment.ironic_twist: The man who would be named 22 years later had once worked as a garage attendant for the same police department hunting him; and the final proof came from a pizza crust at a birthday party

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: How could one man kill for over two decades in the same neighborhood, and why did it take until 2010 to stop him?

the_method._instructions: How did the protagonist do what they did? Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Familial DNA searching of the California offender database + abandoned DNA (discarded pizza crust, napkin, glass)
step_by_step_explanation: Crime-scene DNA from the killings yields a profile with no exact match in the offender databases
California (2008) allows a familial search: look for profiles close enough to be a parent, child or sibling
2008 search: no close relative in the database
2009: son convicted on felony weapons charge; DNA uploaded
April 28, 2010: second search flags the son as a likely close relative
Detectives focus on the father, the right age and living in the area
Undercover officer collects items he discards at a pizza restaurant
Lab compares the DNA to crime-scene evidence: match; arrest July 7, 2010
the_method.why_it_worked: The killer himself was never in the database, but his son entered it in 2009

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: Instead of asking 'is this the man?', the database is asked 'who here could be his son or brother?'
DNA left on things a person throws away, which police may legally collect
Marks a gun leaves on a bullet, like a fingerprint for the weapon

the_method.scale_of_operation: 10 convicted murders and 1 attempted murder over 22 years (1985–2007)

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Los Angeles Police Department and city leadership (as alleged by community advocates and reporters)
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Warn residents of a serial threat, prioritize the killings, keep families informed
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: According to critics, the victims were poor Black women, some affected by drugs or sex work, and were not treated as a priority; LAPD denied indifference
specific_incompetence_examples: 1985: department criticized for not alerting South LA to a possible serial killer earlier (LA Times as summarized by Wikipedia)
1980s: Prescod says she was told by the officer in charge the killer was 'only killing hookers' (her account, KPFK)
Reward in 1986 only raised from $10,000 to $25,000 after pressure
2007: task force formed after DNA link but no public warning (Wikipedia; Pelisek)
Families not told their relatives were linked to a serial killer until press reports (Pelisek)
Nearly six years from arrest to trial (AP; NPR)
Uncharged deaths and missing women never resolved (AP; KPFK)
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The killer had once been a garage attendant for the LAPD; Bernita Sparks (1987) and Janecia Peters (2007) were found in the same alley 20 years apart

the_investigation.investigating_agency: LAPD (task force led by Det. Dennis Kilcoyne) with California Department of Justice DNA lab
the_investigation.operation_code_name_if_any: Not publicly documented (avoid '800 task force' claims unless verified)
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Several serial killers were active in South LA in the 1980s, which complicated linking cases (Kilcoyne, Crime Library); the 'sleep' assumption
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: April 28, 2010 familial search hit to son Christopher Franklin
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Leaving pizza crust, napkin and a glass at a restaurant table
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: Almost 25 years after the first murder (Aug 1985 – July 2010)
